somalia.content: Somalia demands UAE end interference, insists all security agreements go through federal government - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME POLITICS Somalia demands UAE end interference, insists all security agreements go through federal government Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Thursday November 19, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia's federal government has renewed its accusations of interference against the United Arab Emirates, demanding that Abu Dhabi conduct all diplomatic and security engagements through Mogadishu and warning that it will take lawful measures to protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. In a statement issued Wednesday, Nov. 18, Somalia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed serious concern over the continued Emirati interference in the country's internal affairs, accusing the UAE of undermining national unity. advertisements “The Federal Republic of Somalia expresses grave concern over the continued interference of the Government of the United Arab Emirates in Somalia's internal affairs,” the statement said. “This interference undermines Somalia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity.” The ministry reaffirmed that the federal government is the sole authority responsible for Somalia's foreign relations and rejected foreign security arrangements made without its approval. “Somalia reaffirms its rejection of any foreign engagement or parallel security arrangement that bypasses the Federal Government, the sole authority for Somalia's foreign relations,” the statement said. The government called on the UAE to conduct its relations with Somalia exclusively through federal institutions, citing the United Nations Charter and international law. The statement follows a televised address Tuesday by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who accused the UAE of providing political, financial and security support to regional administrations and armed groups that he said were undermining Somalia's unity. Hassan Sheikh also criticized agreements involving the UAE and the administrations of Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, particularly arrangements concerning the strategic ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo. He argued that such agreements must be negotiated through the federal government because the ports are national assets belonging to the Somali people. The president further accused Abu Dhabi of establishing military and security structures outside federal control, allegations that have not been independently verified. Somalia's latest diplomatic statement comes amid an escalating public exchange between officials in Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi. Earlier Wednesday, Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, criticized Hassan Sheikh's remarks, accusing him of prioritizing personal political interests over Somalia's national interests. Gargash defended the UAE's longstanding relationship with Somalia and warned that domestic political rivalries should not draw the country into wider regional disputes. Despite the growing tensions, Somalia's Foreign Ministry emphasized that its objections were directed at the UAE government's policies rather than the Emirati people. “Somalia's concerns relate solely to the policies of the UAE Government, not to the longstanding friendship between the Somali and Emirati peoples,” the ministry said. The government warned that it would pursue lawful measures to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. “The Federal Republic of Somalia will take all necessary lawful measures to safeguard its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity,” the statement concluded. The ministry did not specify what additional measures it intended to take or whether further diplomatic restrictions against the UAE were being considered. The latest confrontation follows Somalia's January decision to terminate agreements with the UAE covering security, defense and economic cooperation, including arrangements involving regional ports. The dispute has intensified amid political disagreements between Mogadishu and several regional administrations over constitutional amendments, power-sharing and the country's electoral process. The UAE maintains economic and security relationships with Somaliland and other Somali regional authorities, while Mogadishu insists that foreign governments must respect the federal government's authority over international relations. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of supporting regional administrations and armed groups that threaten Somalia's integrity, particularly criticizing agreements related to strategic ports that he argues should be negotiated exclusively by the federal government. The UAE's diplomatic adviser, Anwar Gargash, countered these claims, suggesting that the Somali president is prioritizing personal political interests. Despite the escalating tensions, Somalia's Foreign Ministry clarified that its grievances are directed at UAE government policies, not its people, and warned of lawful measures to protect its sovereignty. The UAE has long leveraged its wealth to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, using a mix of economic, military and diplomatic clout to assert regional power. For decades Somalia’s federal government has had only limited authority across the country, and has failed to defeat Islamist militants, despite years of international support, including African peacekeepers and US air strikes. GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said in a statement issued in Riyadh on Thursday that "these unacceptable allegations seek to undermine the UAE's efforts to promote regional and international dialogue and cooperation." The statement did not name the Somalia officials or specify the remarks that prompted the condemnation. Albudaiwi said the UAE had played "a major role in strengthening security and stability and promoting dialogue between countries." He pointed to its recent hosting of a round of talks between Russia and Ukraine as evidence of what he called "a responsible approach aimed at achieving regional and international peace and security." The GCC chief said the bloc "categorically rejects any media campaigns aimed at disparaging any of its members" and said such campaigns "will not affect their continued role in supporting peace and security in the region and around the world." He said the council's member states remained committed to strengthening security, stability and prosperity. The six-member bloc comprises Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. تجمع الهلال حامل اللقب بنظيره الأهلي مروي على ملعب كريمة الأولمبي ضمن الجولة الأولى. ويواجه اتحاد كرة القدم المحلي صعوبات جسيمة في إنجاح المنافسة، في ظل أزمة متجذرة تتمثل في عدم جاهزية الملاعب المضيفة تعاني من ضعف الجاهزية، ما يضع الاتحاد وأندية الدوري أمام تحديات مضاعفة لإنجاح الموسم في ظل الظروف المتاحة، آملين في عودة النشاط تدريجيا، والتمهيد لمرحلة مقبلة تتسم بتجهيزات مبكرة وفق توجه جديد
